source.title: The Anatomy of Alignment: Decomposing Preference Optimization by Steering Sparse Features
source.authors: J. Ferrao; Matthijs van der Lende; Ilija Lichkovski; Clement Neo

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses pretrained SAEs on Gemma-2 models and measures SAE-feature activations and the effects of disabling feature interventions. This is an indirect, different-method test of V4's claim that SAE dictionaries can provide usable sparse features in LLMs. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry or feature-capacity competition.
record.gate_note: The relevant reported results are the feature-composition and feature-ablation measurements in Tables 2 and 3, and base-model feature activation mass in Table 17. The preference, capability, and generation-quality benchmark results are not themselves tests of the representation claims. Hyperparameter sweeps and the linear probe are used for layer or coefficient selection, so are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained GemmaScope SAEs as the control interface for its own method, FSRL. It reports how that adapter's learned policy is composed and what ablating its parts does. It never tests whether SAEs recover the model's features (V4), whether those features are canonical units (V5), or anything about toy superposition, capacity or feature dimensionality. Tables 2 and 3 describe the FSRL steering policy, not the model's natural representation. Table 17 is an activation share of LLM-classified feature groups and does not bear on the existence or recovery of superposed features. The SAE's interpretability is assumed, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that FSRL-based preference optimization 'style-hacks': it relies disproportionately on style/formatting SAE features rather than alignment features, and this degrades coherence. Retraining with style features masked partially restores generation quality and raises TruthfulQA. They present FSRL as a diagnostic tool whose conclusions depend on SAE quality and on an LLM feature classifier with moderate agreement with a human annotator.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce Toy Models of Superposition. It trains a dynamic adapter to steer pretrained SAE features in Gemma-2 models and measures feature-category activations and intervention effects; it does not construct toy networks or test superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effects vary by model scale and dataset: base-model style-feature activation mass differs between the 2B and 9B models, and the style-feature ablation effects differ between models. Feature classification agreement also varies by model and category.

fits_no_version.finding: In the 2B model, LLM-classified style SAE features carry about 50% of L1 activation mass, versus 15-20% in 9B. The authors read this as the 2B style features being 'central and polysemantic'. Ablating both feature categories together raises preference loss non-additively, which they read as style/alignment entanglement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The degree of entanglement or centrality of SAE feature groups differs with model scale (Gemma-2 2B vs 9B).

record.problems: Only Gemma-2-2B-it and Gemma-2-9B-it are studied, with pretrained GemmaScope SAEs. The authors state that SAE feature quality and generalizability are open issues, and report moderate human–LLM classifier agreement (MCC scores 0.448 to 0.764). The feature-category ablations affect the trained FSRL adapter's steering, not the underlying base model representation. Core feature-ablation and activation-mass tables report no uncertainty values.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant rows omitted. Benchmark results, generation win rates, hyperparameter sweeps, and probe accuracies were left out because they do not measure the claim versions' representation properties.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity transition, no geometry.
All: no test of capacity competition causing polysemanticity.
All: the paper calls 2B style features 'polysemantic' by interpretation only, with no test of the cause.
All: the SAEs are used as given; there is no test of feature recovery, reconstruction fidelity, or feature spread across neurons.
All: completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features are not tested; the authors flag SAE quality as a limitation.
All: decoder directions are used as 1-D features without any test.

record.verdict_notes: This is a tool-use study. SAE interpretability is the premise of the method, not its subject. Its 'polysemantic' and 'entanglement' claims are post-hoc interpretations of activation shares and ablation non-additivity, not tests of superposition or of SAE validity. The reader's V4 'supports' label is dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more sparse features than dimensions, overlapping or nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
The paper discusses feature entanglement and calls some SAE features polysemantic, but does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

The study shows that selected pretrained SAE features in two Gemma-2 models have measurable activations and can be used for interventions. It does not test feature recovery fidelity against ground truth, feature spread across neurons, or generality beyond these models and SAEs.
Completeness, stability across training or model changes, and canonicality of SAE features are not empirically tested. The paper notes limitations of SAE quality and generalizability.
The study uses individual decoder-column directions, but does not test whether the model's underlying features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-2B-it and Gemma-2-9B-it; the tested SAE features and datasets reported in Tables 2, 3, and 17
reader_labels.reason: The study measures SAE-feature activations in base models and shows that interventions on selected SAE feature groups change preference loss, providing limited operational evidence that SAE dictionaries expose usable feature directions; see T2-01–T2-24. It does not establish recovery fidelity or canonicality.
